activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
knowledge_domain: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
fact: If prices rise faster than a savings account's interest rate, the money in the account buys less each year even though the balance grows.
story:
Livia taped the last poster to the front of the lemonade stand and counted the jar: eleven dollars and forty cents. The bike at Halvorsen's had a big red sign that said Sale Ends Saturday, which gave her exactly five days. Her savings account held two hundred dollars, and this morning she had asked the cashier at the bike shop, very casually, what the bike cost. "Two sixty-nine," the woman had said, and Livia's stomach had dropped. Two years ago, when she'd started saving, her brother swore that exact bike was two hundred. Her money had been sitting in the bank the whole time, gathering interest. How could it have gotten further away?

"It's a mystery," said Stefan, squeezing lemons beside her. "Like the socks that vanish from the dryer. A parallel mystery. Money goes into a bank, socks go into a dryer, and neither comes out the same."

"It is not the same as socks." Livia poured a cup for a customer, made change, and kept thinking. On paper, her two hundred dollars had grown. She'd even asked Ms. Reddy how the bank added it up, and Ms. Reddy had shown her two ways on a napkin: simple interest, where the bank pays on the original amount every year, and compound, where it pays on the amount plus the interest already earned, so the pile grows faster. Compound won over five years. Livia had walked home pleased. Compound was her friend.

"Then buy the bike with your compound money," said Adeline, arriving with a bag of cups. "Install a basket on it and deliver lemonade. Rolling profits."

"I did the math again last night," Livia said. "Even with compound interest, after five years I'll have maybe two twenty-five. The bike is two sixty-nine." She looked down the street at nothing, then snapped her fingers. "Prices. Prices went up too. Two years ago the bike was two hundred. If prices keep rising faster than my interest, my money buys less every year even though the balance grows. My account is winning and losing at the same time."

"That's a scandal," Adeline said. "A full controversy. The bank should apologize."

"The bank is not going to apologize." Livia grabbed the marker and wrote a new sign: LEMONADE, ONE DOLLAR, HELP LIVIA BEAT THE BIKE SALE BY SATURDAY. Stefan laughed so hard he sloshed the pitcher, and a woman stopped just to ask what beating a bike sale meant. Livia told her the whole thing, socks and all, and the woman bought three cups. Stefan counted the jar every hour and called out the total like a race announcer. By Saturday morning the jar held fifty-two dollars, and Livia stood outside Halvorsen's before it opened, bills folded in her fist, bouncing on her toes.

"I'm winning," she told the door. "Open up."

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: In the Dutch Republic, prices for rare tulip bulbs soared in the winter of 1636 to 1637 and then collapsed in February 1637, when buyers stopped showing up.
story:
The last box of Riftfang trading cards in the whole mall sat behind the glass counter of the game shop, and the price tag read forty euros. Two weeks ago, the same box had cost twelve. Theo counted the money in his pocket twice: twenty-three euros and a bus token.

"Forty," said the cashier, not looking up. "They're going fast."

"Fast because there aren't many," Theo said, "or fast because everyone thinks there aren't many?"

The cashier shrugged. Behind Theo, a boy from another school pressed his face against the glass and asked his mother for fifty euros.

Theo walked out to the fountain and found Esmee and Anouk on the bench beside it. Esmee held her own Riftfang box, still in shrink wrap, on her knees like something fragile.

"They're selling for thirty-five online," Anouk said, scrolling her phone. "Yesterday it was thirty. It keeps climbing."

"Can I buy yours?" Theo asked Esmee. "For twenty-three. That's everything I have."

"Why do you want one so badly?"

"Marcus's birthday is Saturday. Two days. Everyone's bringing Riftfang cards, and if I show up with socks, I'll be the joke of the year." He assessed the situation out loud, because saying it helped him think. "The whole grade wants these cards right now, and the cards are hard to get, so the price goes up. That's the whole problem in one sentence."

Anouk lowered her phone. "You know what this reminds me of? Mr. Janssen told us about it last term. In the Dutch Republic, prices for rare tulip bulbs soared in the winter of 1636 to 1637. People paid fortunes for a single bulb."

"Flowers?" Theo said.

"Tulips. And then in February 1637 it all collapsed, because the buyers stopped showing up." Anouk locked her phone. "One day nobody came, and the prices fell apart."

"Then I wait," Theo said. "If the boys stop wanting cards, the price drops, and I can buy a box cheap."

"If you wait," Esmee said, "the party is Saturday, not next month. You have an obligation to bring a present, not a theory."

She was right about the deadline. Theo tapped his pocket, thinking. Then he made a decision: he would not buy the box. He would buy three single cards from the binder in the shop's back corner, the ones nobody wanted because they were common, and he would build Marcus a custom deck out of them. He had traded cards with Marcus all autumn; he knew which combos he liked.

He went back into the shop and flipped through the binder. The singles were fifty cents each. He picked nine, all resilient creatures, cards that stayed in play and got stronger when attacked. At the counter, the cashier raised an eyebrow at the unimpressive stack.

"Smart," he said anyway, ringing them up. "Box prices are for people who panic."

Theo walked out with four euros and fifty cents left and the cards sleeved in a paper bag. Outside, the boy from the other school was still arguing with his mother over the fifty euros.

At home, Theo laid the nine cards across his bed and started arranging them into a deck. Esmee texted him a photo of the shop's online price list: Riftfang boxes, now forty-two euros.

"Still climbing," she wrote.

Theo texted back, "Let it climb."

On Monday, after the party, Anouk ran up to him in the corridor. "The box price dropped. It's twenty-five now. The cashier says nobody's been in all weekend."

Theo slung his bag over his shoulder. "The buyers stopped showing up."

activity: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
knowledge_domain: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
fact: Earth's tilt slowly varies between about 22.1 and 24.5 degrees over a cycle of about 41,000 years.
story:
Elizabeth had exactly one job on Friday: stand in front of Mr. Novák's science class and explain why summer happens. Not "because it's hot," which was Blake's answer and had earned him a look of deep suffering from Mr. Novák. The real reason, the tilt of Earth's axis, and Elizabeth could recite it fine. The problem was that every time she said it out loud, it sounded like magic.

"You lean something over and it gets hot?" her friend Clarissa had said at lunch. "If I tilt my sandwich, does it become lunch in Australia?"

"That's not the same thing," Elizabeth said, though privately she worried that it might be.

After school she found Mr. Novák stacking chairs in the science room and asked if she could borrow the flashlight and the orange Styrofoam ball he kept on his desk. He handed them over with a warning not to draw a face on it, since the last ball had ended up with a mustache and a name. At home she pushed a pencil through the ball to be the axis, leaned the pencil, and shone the flashlight at it in her dark closet, which felt rebellious even though her mother had said it was fine. When the light hit the tilted ball, one half glowed bright and wide, and the other half caught only a thin, slanted strip. There it was. Not the sandwich kind of tilt. The light itself spread differently depending on the lean, and she could see it, actually see it, on the round orange face of the Earth.

On Friday she did the whole thing live, flashlight and ball and a stick of chalk as the sun. "Summer isn't about being closer," she said. "It's about which half gets the direct light. When the north half leans toward the chalk, the light piles up on it. When it leans away, the light thins out, and that's winter." Clarissa squinted at the ball, tilted her head, and then said, "Oh. Oh, that's it? That's actually obvious. Why did nobody show me a ball before?"

Then Mr. Novák asked the question Elizabeth had not planned for. "So. What if Earth leaned more?"

Elizabeth stood there, chalk in hand. She tilted the ball farther. The bright patch shrank and sharpened; the strip of thin light widened. So a bigger lean meant fiercer summers and harsher winters, packed closer together on the globe. She was about to declare this when a memory surfaced from the planetarium field trip in October, the droning narrator and the domed ceiling of stars. The show had asked that exact question, and the answer had not been "Earth always leans the same." Earth's axis slowly wobbles in its lean, between about 22.1 degrees and 24.5 degrees, over a cycle of roughly 41,000 years. She remembered because 41,000 had seemed like an outrageous number, like a lie a planet would tell.

"We're actually leaning a little differently right now than we will be later," she said slowly, working it out as she spoke. "The tilt drifts between about 22.1 and 24.5 degrees, and the whole cycle takes around 41,000 years. So someday summers and winters get a bit fiercer, and other times, milder. We're just somewhere in the middle of the wobble." She held up the ball and the pencil. "Tropical beaches, mild ones, somewhere far in the future. Probably no chance of us surfing then. Low probability of anyone surfing then."

Mr. Novák raised one eyebrow, which for him was applause. Clarissa raised her hand and asked, dead serious, whether the tilt could ever lean so far that Earth rebelled and fell over sideways.

"Twenty-four point five degrees," Elizabeth said. "That's the maximum. The planet has limits, unlike Blake."

"Hey," said Blake, grinning. "Some of us tilt, we just don't commit to it."

Elizabeth set the ball on the desk and gave it one last, gentle spin.

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: Confirmation bias is the tendency to accept claims that fit what we already believe and to doubt claims that do not, without checking either.
story:
Lucy had one job on a rainy Saturday: write a five-paragraph essay on whether school uniforms should be mandatory, due Monday. Instead she was reading a post that said the Riverside Raptors, the team her school would face on Thursday, had been caught using players from another district. She read it twice, smiled, and hit share before the rain outside had even changed rhythm.

A message popped up from Lylah: "Saw that! Told you they were cheaters." Then one from Abbie: "Where did this come from?" Lucy typed back the name of the account, some kid with a raptor emoji in his handle. Abbie sent a link. It was the original post, dated three weeks earlier, from an account that had also claimed Riverside's mascot was hereditary, passed down through one family since 1954, like a crown. The school had voted on the mascot two years ago. Lucy knew that because she'd been in the gym when they counted the ballots, and because the old mascot had been a slightly embarrassing beaver.

She sat back. She had shared it because it sounded right, and it sounded right because she wanted Riverside to lose on Thursday. Last season Riverside had dismantled them, eleven to two, and their coach had done a slow little bow afterward. She scrolled through her own messages from that night: she'd forwarded a different Riverside rumor then too, something about their pitcher's age, and that one had also turned out to be wrong. A pattern, she thought, was like a hidden rule. You couldn't see the rule itself, only the things it left behind. Her rule seemed to be: if it made Riverside look bad, she believed it, and if it made them look fine, she doubted it. Neither time had she checked anything first.

She opened a search window and typed the school district's name plus "roster rules." Ten minutes of actual reading later she found the league page listing every roster from last spring. The Raptors' players were all listed under their real addresses, which were, annoyingly, all in Riverside. She deleted her share. Then, because deleting felt like sweeping the floor with a broom made of feathers, she posted a correction: "That Riverside story isn't true. I checked. I should have checked before I shared it."

Lylah replied with a single word: "Traitor." Abbie replied with "What do you call that thing where you believe stuff just because you want it to be true?" Lucy typed "confirmation bias" and then deleted it, because she wasn't sure that was the whole answer either. Her dad called from the kitchen that dinner was ready and could she please also explain democracy to him, since she seemed to be settling all disputes tonight.

"Still working on it," Lucy called back, and turned to her blank essay document. She typed the title, "Why I Changed My Mind About One Post," and underneath it: "Paragraph one: the rain."

activity: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
knowledge_domain: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
fact: The first call from a handheld cellular phone was made by Motorola engineer Martin Cooper on a New York street on April 3, 1973.
story:
Zoe sat at the kitchen table while her mother slid the box across, and inside was the phone she had waited two years for. The screen lit up when she pressed the button, and the first thing she noticed was a graph already on it, green bars rising and falling. "That's your usage data," her mom said. "I set a rule. You keep it under an hour a day, and you enroll in the phone safety course at school next week." Zoe nodded, but her eyes were on the graph. Why were there bars already? The phone was brand new. Nobody had used it but the store clerk, and he had only tapped a few screens.

She thought about it while texting her friend Zarah, who had a phone of her own and strong opinions about everything. "Come over," Zoe typed, "I have a mystery." When Zarah arrived, she plopped on the couch and said, "Before the mystery, can I ask something? Can we do my history extra credit together? I need it to bump my grade before the semester ends." Zoe said sure, and Zarah pulled out a worksheet with a trivia question printed at the bottom: When was the first call from a handheld cellular phone made, and by whom? Zarah groaned. "I put 1990. And some guy named Cooper, I guessed."

Zoe tilted her head. She picked up her phone, checked the settings, and ran a quick analysis of the usage log, reading the times and apps one by one. Every bar belonged to the same hour, the hour they had been at the store. The clerk must have been downloading updates and setting up the account before handing it over. So the data was the store's, not hers. She tested it by watching the timer while she opened one app for exactly one minute, and the green bar climbed by exactly that much. "It's measuring live," she said. "It's real." Then she searched the trivia question, because now she wanted the answer too.

The screen said the call was made by Motorola engineer Martin Cooper on a New York street on April 3, 1973. "Whoa," Zoe said. "Phones in pockets are older than my mom." Zarah copied it down, checked her earlier guess of 1990, and wrinkled her nose. "I was seventeen years off." She copied it again, carefully, in pen. "I'm getting this one right. Half my class thinks phones were invented in the nineties."

The twist came at dinner, when Mr. Brennan from next door stopped by to borrow a ladder and spotted the phone on the counter. He squinted at it, then laughed. "I remember when that call happened. It was in the news, an engineer walking down a New York street with a phone in his hand, April 3, 1973. Everybody thought it was impossible." Zoe stared at him. He had been alive when nobody had pockets with phones in them at all. "So it wasn't always like this," she said slowly, "everyone reachable everywhere." He shook his head and shouldered the ladder.

Later, alone in her room, Zoe set her own alarm for fifty minutes, five under the limit, so she could never slip past the rule even by accident. Her objective was simple: keep the phone, prove she could handle it, and stay the curious one, the one who noticed the green bars before anyone else did. She typed one last message to Zarah: "Tomorrow, quiz me on Cooper." Then she plugged the phone in, turned the screen facedown, and went to find her mother to ask about the ladder man and his impossible sidewalk call.

activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
knowledge_domain: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
fact: A prime checker must handle numbers below 2 separately, because 0, 1 and negative numbers are not prime, yet a divisor loop starting at 2 finds nothing to reject them.
story:
Nicolas typed RUN and watched the little window blink at him. His program asked for a number, checked it for divisors, and printed whether it was prime, which was exactly what Mr. Rodríguez had assigned. He tried 7. Prime. He tried 9. Not prime. He tried 13. Prime. So far the program was smarter than his little brother, who insisted eleven was "basically a ten."

"Let me try something," said Kenneth, leaning over from the next computer. "Try zero."

Nicolas typed 0. The program thought about it for less than a blink and announced: PRIME.

"Zero is not prime," Kenneth said, laughing so hard he nearly knocked his mouse off the desk. "Even I know that, and I once forgot my own birthday."

"That's weird," Nicolas said. "It didn't find any divisors, so it just said yes." He stared at the loop in his code, the one that started counting at 2 and looked for numbers that divided evenly into whatever he typed. The loop never rejected anything smaller than where it started looking. It was like checking a backpack for smuggled sandwiches by starting at the second pocket. He tried 1. PRIME. He tried negative five. PRIME, again, cheerfully confident, completely wrong.

Mackenna wandered over with her laptop balanced on one arm. "What's so funny over here?"

"Nicolas invented a new kind of math," Kenneth said.

Nicolas rubbed his chin. Was there a hidden rule here, a pattern he hadn't noticed? Numbers below 2 were the problem, that much he could see. His loop started at 2, so it never tested anything smaller, which meant 0, 1, and the negative numbers sailed straight through. He wondered if every program that checked for primes had to deal with this, or if it was only his. Probably every one, he decided, since the pattern wasn't about his code, it was about numbers themselves.

Mr. Rodríguez strolled past and paused, reading over Nicolas's shoulder. "You look systematic about something," he said.

"Nicolas's program thinks zero is prime," Kenneth reported, delighted.

"I authorized exactly this kind of discovery," Mr. Rodríguez said, tapping the screen where the loop began. "Fix it."

Nicolas added a line before the loop: if the number was less than 2, print NOT PRIME. He typed 0 and pressed ENTER. NOT PRIME. He tried 1 and negative five. Both NOT PRIME, both correct at last. Then, just to be sure the whole concept hadn't broken somewhere else, he tried 13 again.

PRIME.

"Perfect," Nicolas said, and Kenneth clapped once, loudly, like a seal who had just been told good news.

activity: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
knowledge_domain: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
fact: Pasta releases starch into its cooking water, and a splash of that starchy water helps a sauce thicken and cling to the pasta.
story:
Katherine stood at Lucille's kitchen counter with an onion and a very sharp knife, which felt like a bad combination. Lucille's grandmother's sauce recipe was taped to the cabinet, and tonight they were making it themselves because Lucille wanted, more than anything, to prove she could cook a real dinner before her older sister came home from college. "Claw grip," Katherine said, curling her fingertips under like talons so the knuckles, not the fingertips, would guide the blade. "My mom showed me a video, but I've never actually done it." She brought the knife down and the onion split cleanly in half, which felt like a small victory.

"That's better than my first try," Lucille said. "I cried for ten minutes and thought I was dying." Katherine laughed, then blinked hard, because the onion fumes were getting to her too. She persisted anyway, slicing slowly, her knuckles bumping the flat of the blade the way the video promised they would. The rings came apart on the cutting board, wet and pale, and she said, "Those look like larva casings, honestly," and Lucille made a face and said, "Do not say that about food we're eating." The cuts were uneven at first, thick chunks and papery slivers, but by the second half of the onion they came out even, and Lucille pointed and said, "Look, you're getting an intricate little pattern going."

They dropped the onions into hot oil and the kitchen began to smell like a restaurant. Lucille stirred while Katherine read the recipe over her shoulder. The tomatoes went in, then salt, then a long wait while the sauce burped and spat. Meanwhile the pasta boiled away in the big pot next to it. When a strand tasted soft, Lucille grabbed the pot and swung it toward the sink to dump it all out.

"Wait," Katherine said, grabbing a mug. She'd noticed something: the water wasn't clear like tap water. It was cloudy, almost milky. "The pasta leaves starch in that water. A splash of it helps the sauce thicken and stick to the pasta." She'd read it somewhere and half forgotten it, but the cloudy water was proof sitting right in front of her. "We can test it." She scooped a cupful before Lucille could pour the rest down the drain, and they spooned a little into the tomato sauce. Within a minute or two it went from thin and runny to glossy, and when they tossed the pasta through it, every strand came out coated instead of slick and bare.

Lucille's sister walked in the door right as they set the plates down, sniffed the air, and said, "You two made this?" Katherine lifted her fork. "Try it," she said.

activity: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time
knowledge_domain: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time
fact: Stacking hot flatbreads inside a clean cloth keeps them warm and soft by trapping their steam.
story:
Alyssa stood in her grandmother's kitchen with three timers going at once, and she was starting to dread all of them. The rice needed twenty minutes, the curry needed to simmer for forty, and the flatbread had to be cooked one at a time on the hot pan, which meant she could not just start everything together. Her grandmother had gone to the garden, saying only, "You'll work it out, beta." Alyssa drew a plan on the back of a receipt: start the curry first, then the rice, then make the breads last, while the other pots rested with their lids on. She was proud of how systematic it looked, even if her handwriting slanted downhill.

The curry bubbled and filled the kitchen with the smell of cumin and coconut. The rice pot hissed softly under its lid. Alyssa rolled her first flatbread thin, slapped it onto the pan, and watched it puff up like a small balloon. "Yes," she whispered, flipping it. She slid it onto an open plate by the stove and started the next one.

By the time the third bread came off the pan, she picked up the first one and frowned. It had gone stiff, its edges curled and dry like an old leaf. She bent it and it cracked along the middle. Her plan was working for the rice and the curry, both steaming and ready together, but the bread was turning into a failure right in front of her, one flat piece at a time. She thought about the rice, how the lid kept it soft, and about the steam that had curled up from each bread when she lifted it off the pan. The steam was escaping off the open plate, and the bread was drying out. That had to be the hidden cause.

She fetched a clean cloth napkin, stacked her hot flatbreads inside it, and folded the edges over the top like a little parcel. Then she cooked the last two breads and tucked them in too, quickly, so the steam stayed caught inside. When her grandmother came back in, shaking dirt from the tomatoes, Alyssa set the table and held her breath.

The rice was fluffy, the curry was thick and fragrant, and when Alyssa unwrapped the cloth, the flatbreads were still warm, soft and bendable, just as they came off the pan. Her grandmother tore one, dipped it into the curry, and nodded. "Better than my first attempt, I'll admit. Mine came out like roof tiles."

Alyssa laughed so hard she nearly dropped the spoon, and then she reached for a second flatbread while it was still steaming.

activity: to calculate the resistance of a wire from measured voltage and current using Ohm's law
knowledge_domain: to calculate the resistance of a wire from measured voltage and current using Ohm's law
fact: For wires of the same material and thickness, doubling the length doubles the resistance.
story:
Raphael crouched at the edge of the bowls with a battery pack, two lengths of thin copper wire, a meter, and a notebook that was already curling from the heat. Carly rolled up beside him and kicked her board into her hand.

"Still married to the resistor thing?" she asked.

"Ms. Chanthavong says I can retake the practical if I show her real measurements by Friday," Raphael said. "I have to calculate resistance from voltage and current. Ohm's law. Divide volts by amps." He clipped the shorter wire into his little circuit, a battery and a small bulb, and touched the meter probes to each end. The bulb glowed and the screen showed him the numbers he needed. He scribbled them down.

Krish arrived with a bottle of water and watched over Raphael's shoulder. "So what's the second wire for?"

"Same thickness, same stuff, but it's twice as long," Raphael said. "I want to see if length matters." He swapped it in. The bulb came up dimmer, which made him sit straighter, and when he worked through the arithmetic his pencil stopped halfway through the line. The resistance had come out double. He checked the division twice, because a meter could be off or his hand could shake, but the number sat there stubborn as a stain. He measured the shorter piece again, then the longer one, then laid both wires on the flat concrete, held perpendicular to each other so their ends lined up at one corner, and confirmed the long one really was two of the short one. Its resistance really was two of the other one too.

"Say that again," Krish said, crouching to look.

"For wires of the same material and thickness, doubling the length doubles the resistance." Raphael said it slowly, the way you test a board before you commit your weight to it. "Every time. That's the pattern."

"That's actually a principle," Carly said. "Like, a real rule, not just your two wires."

"It's two wires so far," Raphael said, but he grinned and wrote the rule at the top of a fresh page. Then he borrowed a third piece from his kit, half the length of the short one, and predicted the resistance before touching a probe. When the meter matched his prediction almost exactly, he pumped his fist and Carly smacked his shoulder.

"Ms. Chanthavong is going to eat this up," Krish said.

On Friday Raphael set out his notebook on the lab bench, wires coiled on top, and walked Ms. Chanthavong through each measurement, pointing at the numbers instead of reading them off the page. When he reached the doubled wire, he tapped the column of results and said, "Watch this part."

activity: trying out for a school sports team
knowledge_domain: trying out for a school sports team
fact: Losing about 2 percent of body weight in sweat without drinking enough can noticeably reduce athletic performance, especially in endurance events.
story:
The locker room smelled like chlorine and rubber sandals, and Logan sat on the bench retaping his goggles while voices bounced off the lockers. In twenty minutes the coach would post the final list for the swim team, and one spot was still open between him and Emilie. He watched her dig through her bag twice, then a third time, her hands moving faster each pass. "My water bottle," she said. "It's not here. I left it on the counter at home." She said it like it was nothing, but Logan had spent all season noticing small things, and this one irritated him, the way a pebble in a shoe irritates a runner, because it seemed bigger than it sounded.

They'd been at the pool for two hours of tryouts already, and the coach had warned them the last heat would be the longest, four hundred meters, no breaks. Logan kept turning the problem over. Emilie was the strongest swimmer in their grade; her splits had been consistent all morning, lap after lap within a second of each other. But he'd also noticed that she sweated heavily even in the water, and she'd had nothing to drink since breakfast. He tried to picture it like the erosion he'd studied in science, the way a little water moving over stone, given enough time, wears the whole shape of a canyon away. If something small kept being taken out of her, hour after hour, what would be left by the final heat?

"Emilie," he said quietly, so the others wouldn't hear, "how much do you weigh?" She gave him a look. "Why?" "Just tell me." "Fifty kilos, roughly." He did the math on his palm with a fingertip. Two percent of fifty kilos was one kilo. She'd been sweating for two hours with nothing going back in, and she probably wasn't far off that. He'd read it in an old magazine in the dentist's office, and it had stuck with him because it surprised him: losing about 2 percent of your body weight in sweat without drinking enough can noticeably reduce your performance, especially in endurance events. A four-hundred-meter heat was an endurance event if anything was.

"There's a drinking fountain by the equipment cage," he said. "You've got ten minutes. Drink as much as you can hold." She hesitated, glancing toward the pool where the coach was lining up lane ropes, and Logan could see her weighing it: accept help from the boy competing for her spot, or ignore him. "Why are you telling me this?" she asked. "Because if you fade out there, I'll never know if I actually beat you," he said. "I want it to be real." That, he realized as he said it, was true.

She drank for two full minutes, then came back wiping her mouth. The whistle blew. In the last hundred meters, when Logan's arms felt like wet rope, Emilie pulled even with him, then ahead by half a body length, and her stroke never fell apart the way it had in his imagination. They touched the wall one after the other, gasping. Later, in the locker room, the coach taped the list inside the door. Both their names were on it. Emilie bumped his shoulder with hers and said, "Next time, remind me before hour one, not hour two."

activity: to compare a first-past-the-post election with proportional representation using a sample vote count
knowledge_domain: to compare a first-past-the-post election with proportional representation using a sample vote count
fact: Proportional representation more often produces coalition governments, because a single party rarely wins more than half the votes.
story:
Maria had promised Ms. Wilson she would explain the vote count to everyone at the town hall meeting, and now the moment had arrived and her hands were sweating on the photocopies. The community room smelled of coffee and floor wax, and forty folding chairs held late-arriving neighbours, along with Sloane and Angie from her class, who waved from the back row. Ms. Wilson had set up two tables side by side, and on each table sat a shoebox of ballots from the mock election the students had run that afternoon, when four pretend parties had competed for the town's ten council seats.

Maria cleared her throat and held up the first chart. "Under first past the post, the town is divided into ten districts," she said. "In each district, whoever gets the most votes wins the seat." She read out the results slowly, tracing each column with her finger. The Blue party had won five seats, the Green party three, and the Orange and Purple parties one each, even though the Orange party had taken nearly a quarter of the overall votes. A man in a green jacket frowned at his handout, and Maria noticed his eyes jumping between the seat totals and the percentage of votes each party had received. Was he seeing the same gap she had seen in class, that the seats didn't match the votes?

"Now we count the same ballots the proportional way," she said, moving to the second table. Sloane came up to help, sliding ballots into bundles, and the whispering in the room quieted as the stacks grew. When they finished, Maria wrote the new numbers on the flip chart: Blue had four seats, Green three, Orange two, and Purple one. She stared at it for a second, because something was missing. Blue had been shut out of a majority. Under first past the post they'd controlled half the seats plus one, but here, no single party held more than half.

"So who runs the council?" Angie called out from the back.

"That's exactly it," Maria said. "Nobody can. Blue has to talk to Green or Orange and share power." She turned to the flip chart and added a column headed "coalition." A grey-haired woman near the front said she'd always wondered why some countries seemed to govern in teams, and Maria realized the shoebox of paper ballots had somehow managed to convey something she'd only understood this week herself: that when seats follow votes proportionally, one party rarely ends up with more than half, so the parties have to negotiate.

The man in the green jacket raised his hand. "Under this system, would my Orange vote have counted twice as much?"

Maria checked the numbers, twice, the way Ms. Wilson had taught her to be competent rather than fast. "Twice as many seats, from the same votes," she said. He nodded slowly and wrote something in his notebook. Sloane leaned over the table and whispered, "Do it again with three parties?" Maria was already pulling the rubber band off the next stack of ballots.

activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
knowledge_domain: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
fact: Near the ends of long bones are growth plates made of cartilage, where bones lengthen during childhood; a break through a growth plate can affect how the bone grows.
story:
The skateboard had slipped out from under Mathis at the top of the school ramp, and now he sat on a squeaky plastic chair in the emergency room with his left arm resting on a pillow in his lap. Katelynn had come with him on the bus because his mom's shift wouldn't end until nine. The waiting room smelled like disinfectant and coffee, and the thermostat on the wall behind the reception desk was set so low that Mathis could see goosebumps on Katelynn's arms.

"Stop wiggling your fingers," she said. "You'll irritate the splint."

"It itches." He wiggled them anyway, just to prove the arm still obeyed him. The fingers were swollen but pink, and being pink, he had decided, was a good sign. In the corner, a toddler stacked and knocked over the same three magazines over and over.

When the X-rays came back, the doctor clipped them onto a lightbox and pointed with a pen. "You broke the radius, one of the two bones in your forearm," she said. "The good news is that the break missed the growth plate."

Mathis leaned closer. The bone on the screen looked like a pale stick with a dark crack running across it, but near his wrist he could see a faint darker band. "That's the growth plate?"

"Near the ends of your long bones," the doctor said. "Cartilage, not bone yet. That's where the bone lengthens while you're growing."

"So if the crack went through that part," Mathis said slowly, working it out, "the bone might not grow right afterward."

"That's why we check so carefully," she said, and drew a small circle around the crack with her pen. "Yours is safely above it."

The cast went on in a small room that smelled like warm plaster. The technician dipped strips of cloth in water and wound them around Mathis's arm while the radio played something soft and old. The plaster began to heat up as it dried, which surprised him until Katelynn said it was a chemical thing, like hand warmers in winter.

"Green or blue?" the technician asked.

"Blue," Mathis said.

"You realize people are going to sign that thing for the next six weeks," Katelynn said. "Blair is going to draw a mustache on it. I'm telling you now so it won't be a shock."

"That is not feasible," Mathis said. "I'll keep a marker in my good hand at all times."

When his mom finally arrived, out of breath and still in her work vest, the technician handed Mathis a sling and a printed sheet about keeping the cast dry. On the way out through the sliding doors, the night air felt warm after the freezing waiting room, and Mathis pressed his palm carefully against the hard blue shell, still faintly warm as fresh bread.

activity: getting a first pair of glasses
knowledge_domain: getting a first pair of glasses
fact: 20/40 vision means you must stand 20 feet away to read letters that a person with normal eyesight can read from 40 feet.
story:
Isla sat in the waiting room of the optometrist's office with a plastic paddle over one eye, reading letters off a screen across the hall. Her friend Benedict had come along because his little brother had a lesson nearby, and he was supposed to be her math tutor that afternoon anyway, so they had brought the workbook.

"Second line," said the technician.

Isla squinted. The E was obvious. The F could have been a P. "F," she guessed, and it was wrong, and the next two were wrong too. She heard Benedict snicker behind her and elbowed backwards without turning around.

The optometrist flipped lenses into the big frame and asked her to evaluate each one: better or worse, clearer or blurrier. Finally she wrote something on a card and turned it around. "Twenty forty, both eyes."

"Forty?" Benedict sat up. "That's better than twenty twenty, right? Bigger number."

The optometrist started to open her mouth, but Isla got there first, because something about the card was nagging at her. The letters on the screen were tiny from where she sat, and the technician had said something about the viewing distance earlier. Twenty feet. She looked at the card again, then at the hallway, doing the arithmetic in her head.

"No," she said slowly. "It's the other way around. It means I have to stand twenty feet away to read letters a person with normal eyes can read from forty. The bigger the second number, the worse it is." She waited until the optometrist nodded once, then felt her ears go hot. She had spent half of last term bragging that her eyesight was probably excellent because she could see the board fine, mostly, if she leaned forward.

"So all those times you copied off my homework," Benedict said, "you literally couldn't see the board."

"You said you didn't mind."

"I didn't say that. You couldn't read the board, so you couldn't read my face either."

The frames they chose were thin and dark, and when Isla put them on in the hallway, the world sharpened like someone had wiped a window. She could see individual leaves on the potted fern by the reception desk, lush and deeply green, each frond separate instead of one soft blob. She could see the numbers on the elevator buttons across the lobby. She could see Benedict's face, clearly, and the exact expression on it, which was something she had never once been able to make out from across a room.

He looked bored. He looked like he was already leaving.

"Hey," she called down the hallway, "wait, is that actually what you look like when I talk?"

activity: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
knowledge_domain: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
fact: In hot deserts, the sun and dry air could evaporate far more water in a year than falls as rain, so the ground stays dry.
story:
Grandma's house sat at the edge of a town where the lawns had given up and everyone's plumbing ran to a patch of gravel with one brave cactus in the middle. Emilia had brought her climate project with her: two graphs, rainfall bars and temperature lines, one for a rainforest in Brazil and one for this desert. The rainforest's rainfall bars were so tall they bent off the page; the desert's were little stumps you could count on one hand.

Her grandmother had said, mysterious as always, "Measure the rain while you're here. See what you find." Emilia suspected this meant nothing would fall at all, which would be a short experiment.

At nine in the morning, on the advice of Jazlyn on a video call, Emilia poured a bucket of water into the low spot behind the garage, making a puddle the size of a dinner plate. "That's your rainforest," Jazlyn said. "Ten bars of rainfall, all at once. Take a picture every hour." Emilia marked the puddle's edge with pebbles and set her ruler in the middle, then went inside to study the graphs.

By ten, the pebble ring enclosed a puddle the size of a salad plate. By eleven, a saucer. The temperature line on the desert graph climbed toward its afternoon peak, and Emilia stood at the window thinking about what she couldn't see directly. Nothing was soaking this water away; the ground under the puddle was dry a centimeter down, she'd checked. Nothing was drinking it. So the water had to be leaving upward, into air that was hot and, according to the graph, got barely any rain all year to replace it. She did the arithmetic on a napkin: at this rate, the ground here could lose far more water in a year by evaporation than the sky ever handed back. That was why the ground stayed dry. The stumpy little bars weren't just small; they were outmatched.

She video-called Jazlyn and Trevor and held up the napkin. "The desert loses more water than it gets. The rainforest gets more than it can lose. They're like opposite problems."

"So your conclusion is that your puddle got robbed," Trevor said.

"Evaporated," Emilia said. "But yes."

"It feels like this violates some rule of science," Jazlyn said, squinting at the napkin through the camera. "Water shouldn't just leave."

"Tell that to my puddle."

At lunchtime Emilia went out with her ruler one last time. The pebbles sat in a neat little circle around hot, pale gravel, and a lizard had climbed onto the flattest one, as if the experiment had been arranged entirely for its comfort. She photographed the crime scene, wrote "noon: zero centimeters" in her notebook, and put a pebble in her pocket for evidence.

activity: trying out for a school sports team
knowledge_domain: trying out for a school sports team
fact: All 50 U.S. states, and Washington, D.C., have passed laws on handling concussions in youth sports.
story:
The gymnasium smelled like floor wax and old sweat, and the basketballs thumping across the hardwood made an ominous drumroll that Lily felt in her ribs. Forty girls had come to tryouts, and only twelve would make the roster. She had practiced her crossover all summer for this.

Halfway through the scrimmage, Kaelyn went up for a rebound, took an elbow, and landed hard on her tailbone. Her head snapped back and cracked against the floor. The whistle shrieked, and Ms. Zhu waved everyone to the water cooler while she crouched beside Kaelyn. Lily jogged over with Kaelyn's water bottle, because Kaelyn's hands were shaking too badly to grip it.

"They want to send you to the nurse," Camila reported, sidling up to Lily. "Kaelyn says she's fine, but Ms. Zhu won't budge."

"That's weird," Lily said. "When I sprained my wrist last year, my mom had to sign a form before I could play again. I thought that was just our school being careful." She frowned, turning it over. It wasn't just their school, though. Her cousin in Ohio had told her almost the same story, and a girl at basketball camp from Georgia, too. Same form, same nurse, same sitting out. That was too much of a coincidence. "It's like there's a rule everywhere," she said slowly. "Like somebody wrote it down and every school has to follow it."

Lily crept close enough to hear Ms. Zhu say to Kaelyn, "It's not my choice, and it's not the school's. All fifty states, and Washington, D.C., have passed laws on handling concussions in youth sports. Wherever you play, this is the law. You sit out until a doctor clears you."

Kaelyn groaned. "So I miss the tryout and the whole season."

"You miss today," Ms. Zhu said. "The season is long."

Lily thought about that all through the last drill. If the rule was everywhere, then hiding a knock to the head wouldn't help anyone, not here, not on any team in any state. So when Lily went for a loose ball, banged heads with a girl in a green headband, and felt the gym tilt sideways like a boat, she didn't shake it off. She walked straight to Ms. Zhu and said, "I think I got my bell rung. I'm seeing two of that banner."

Ms. Zhu sat her down, called the nurse, and appointed Lily to keep the score sheet for the rest of tryouts so she'd still feel part of things. Lily tallied baskets while the room slowly stopped rocking.

A week later, the roster went up. Lily's name was on it. So was Kaelyn's, with a note: cleared by a doctor, evaluation to follow.

"Wait," Lily said, staring at the list. "You're on the team and I'm on the team, and we both spent tryouts on a bench."

Kaelyn grinned and tossed her a ball. "Best seat I ever played from."

activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
knowledge_domain: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
fact: The Sieve of Eratosthenes, an ancient Greek method, lists primes by crossing out the multiples of each prime in turn.
story:
Lauren sat at the kitchen table with her laptop open and a pencil behind her ear. Her program was supposed to ask for a number and print whether it was prime, but when she typed 9, it said PRIME, which was wrong. She knew 9 was 3 times 3. She had tested 2, 3, 5, 7 and 11, and all of those had come out right, so the problem was hiding somewhere between the numbers that worked and the ones that didn't.

"Try 25," said Lochlan, who was across the table with a cookie he hadn't been offered. "If it says that's prime too, then your loop is stopping too early."

Lauren typed 25. NOT PRIME, the screen said. She leaned back and stared at it. "So 9 is wrong but 25 is right. That's backwards. Bigger numbers should be harder, not easier."

"It's symmetrical in a weird way," Lochlan said, looking at the screen from an angle. "9 works wrong, 25 works right. Maybe try 49." She did, and 49 came out right too. Only 9 was lying. She adjusted the indentation of one line, moving the print statement out of the loop, and 9 still came out wrong, so it wasn't that. Then she counted her loop's steps on her fingers and found it: her loop checked divisors up to half the number, which worked for 25 because 5 is exactly half, but 3 was less than half of 9 and the loop never got the comparison right. She fixed it and ran the whole list of numbers from 2 to 50.

"Great," said Malika, who had arrived in time to eat the cookie. "But how do you know the program's right now? You can't just trust it because it fixed one bug." She pulled a sheet of graph paper from her backpack and drew a grid of the numbers 1 to 50. "My grandfather showed me this. You cross out 1, then for each prime in turn you cross out all its multiples. It's called the Sieve of Eratosthenes, some old Greek thing." She crossed out every second number after 2, then every third number after 3, and handed the pencil to Lauren.

Lauren crossed out the multiples of 5, then 7, watching the pattern spread down the grid like a net. When she finished, the numbers left standing were the primes. She read them out one by one, 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, all the way to 47, while Lochlan checked each answer against the program's output on the screen. They matched, line for line, all fifteen of them.

"Every single one," Lochlan said. "Same order, same numbers." Lauren copied the grid into her notebook and folded it into her pocket, then typed one more number into the program, 97, just to see.

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: Akira Kurosawa's 1950 film Rashomon tells one crime through four witnesses whose accounts contradict each other.
story:
The art room window had been broken since Monday, and by Wednesday morning Ms. Do had posted a notice on the door: whoever broke it should come forward. Nolan hadn't broken it, but he'd been the last one in the room, so the whole school seemed to have decided he had. He wanted his name cleared before the principal's meeting on Friday.

He decided to invest his lunch period in finding out what had actually happened. Four people had seen something: Brendon, Caitlyn, a seventh grader from the drama club, and the custodian. He tracked them down one by one in the cafeteria and the hallway outside the gym.

Brendon said a tall kid in a gray hoodie threw a rock from the parking lot and ran. Caitlyn said the window cracked on its own while the wind was slamming the side door, no rock anywhere. The seventh grader swore he saw Ms. Do's cart tip against the glass, and the custodian muttered that a ladder from the roofers had slipped and come down hard on the frame. Every account sounded certain. Every account contradicted the others.

Nolan remembered something Ms. Do had said once, about a movie she'd shown her film class. It was called Rashomon, made in 1950, and it told one crime through four witnesses whose accounts all contradicted each other. At the time he'd thought that was just a movie thing, but standing in the hallway he understood it was a people thing. So he tested a simple idea: if someone really saw it, they'd know details only visible from where they stood. He asked each witness what color the tape on the window frame was. Caitlyn, who'd been in the room, said the frame had no tape at all. Brendon said blue. The seventh grader said silver. The custodian just said he hadn't looked.

The seventh grader's story fell apart fast after that. He'd been in the parking lot, nowhere near the cart, and when Nolan pointed out the art room had no cart, the kid went pale and admitted he'd heard about the window secondhand from his sister and made up the rest. But that still left three stories and one broken window. On Friday morning Nolan stood outside the principal's office with his notes, and Caitlyn beside him, ready to say her piece. The door opened and the principal looked out at both of them.

"You've got five minutes," she said, and held the door wide.

activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
knowledge_domain: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
fact: Chlorine bleach must never be mixed with cleaners containing ammonia, because together they release chloramine, a toxic gas.
story:
Felix stood in front of the washing machine with his father's note in one hand and a heap of clothes on the floor. The note said, "Dark clothes together, whites separate, one scoop, cold water," which seemed simple until he pulled his brother's grass-stained soccer shirt from the pile and a red sock migrated from the dark side to the white side all by itself, or so it looked. He snatched the sock back and told himself the whites would not turn pink on his watch.

The real trouble was the stain on the white shirt. Felix carried both bottles from the cabinet above the sink to the kitchen table, where the light was better: a bottle of chlorine bleach and a spray bottle of the ammonia cleaner his mother used on the counters. He planned to pour a little of each into the same bucket of water and let the shirt soak, because two cleaners had to be twice as good as one. He reached for the caps.

Then he paused. He was the kid whose class had made him "safety ambassador" in science last spring, mostly because he was the only one who actually read the handouts, and something about the small print on the bleach bottle was tugging at him. He turned the bottle and read: do not mix with cleaners containing ammonia. He picked up the spray bottle and found the word ammonia right there on the front label. He stood very still in the kitchen with both bottles in his hands, thinking about how close he had come.

He set them down on opposite ends of the table, like two kids who could not sit together. When Mr. Morin from next door knocked to return a casserole dish, Felix opened the door still holding the bleach. "Careful with that," Mr. Morin said, nodding at the bottle. "My brother mixed bleach and ammonia once in a restaurant kitchen. The gas is called chloramine, and it's toxic. Sent two cooks outside coughing." Felix said he had read the labels just in time, and Mr. Morin raised an eyebrow and said, "Good. Most people don't."

After the door closed, Felix thought about last summer, when he had dumped dish soap into the dishwasher just to be helpful, and the kitchen had flooded with defiant white bubbles that climbed right over the machine's edge. He had not read anything that day. He had just poured. Maybe that was the pattern: things you cannot see, like what two liquids do inside a bucket, follow rules whether or not you know them, and the labels are the only place the rules show themselves.

He filled a bucket with water and bleach alone, soaked the shirt, and watched the grass stain fade to a pale shadow. Then he ran the dark load, cold water, one scoop, and folded everything on the table while it was still warm, matching socks into pairs. His mother came home and picked up the folded soccer shirt. "You did all this?" she asked. "Every load, every sock," Felix said, and slid the two bottles, still at opposite ends of the table, safely back into the cabinet, one at a time.

activity: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
knowledge_domain: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
fact: The formula =SUM(B2:B10) adds every cell from B2 to B10; the colon between the two cells marks a range.
story:
Rachel's mom had said she could use the spare desk in the corner of her office as long as she stayed quiet, so Rachel spread her notebook out beside the keyboard and frowned at the mess of numbers inside it. All week she and Jayson and Jaxxon had run a lemonade stand outside Jaxxon's house, and every day they had scribbled sales on a crumpled sheet that was starting to deteriorate, the ink smudged and the paper torn at the fold. By Friday the crumple had turned into an argument. Jayson swore they had sold forty-one cups; Jaxxon insisted it was thirty-eight; and Rachel had a sinking feeling in her conscience, because she was the one who had lost Tuesday's slip of paper somewhere between the porch and the trash bin.

"I'm fixing it for real," she announced, booting up the computer while her mom was in a meeting down the hall. "Ms. Le showed my class these things once. You put the numbers in boxes, and the machine does the adding."

Jaxxon had biked over after dinner, and he leaned on the back of her chair, breathing mint gum air over her shoulder. "Boxes won't find Tuesday's cups," he said.

"No, but Mom's coworker kept the receipt book at the front desk, remember? They bought cups from the office supply closet." Rachel had already dug the little pink receipt out of her backpack, which made her feel a lot better about losing the slip. Two lemonades, one large, one small, all legitimate sales with a paper trail. She typed Monday into the first row, then Tuesday, then straight down until Friday's total sat in the tenth row.

Then came the hard part. She knew the numbers had to add up, but she wasn't going to add them in her head like some caveman. She clicked an empty cell, typed an equals sign, and then hesitated. Ms. Le had said something once about a shortcut, something short. Rachel typed =B2+B3+B4+B5+B6+B7+B8+B9+B10, stared at it, and thought, there has to be a better way than this. She remembered Ms. Le drawing two little dots on the whiteboard between two cell names. A colon, she'd called it. Rachel deleted the whole long line and tried instead =SUM(B2:B10). When she pressed Enter, the number 39 popped into the box, and she grabbed Jaxxon's sleeve.

"Look. It counted every box from B2 all the way down to B10. Two dots, that's all it takes." She slid the receipt closer, checked the pink column against her screen, and the total held. Thirty-nine cups, and Tuesday's two were right there in it.

"So Jayson was wrong and so was I," Jaxxon said, "by exactly one cup each." He tapped the screen. "Can it draw? Like a picture of the week?"

Rachel found the chart button, highlighted her numbers, and clicked. Five bars grew upward across the screen, Saturday's bar standing tallest, Tuesday's a stubby little nub. Down the hall a door opened, and her mom's voice carried around the corner.

"Rachel? Is that a bar chart on my work computer?"

"It's a lemonade chart," Rachel called back. "Saturday's the big one. Want to see what a colon can do?"

activity: to improvise a blues solo over a twelve-bar chord progression
knowledge_domain: to improvise a blues solo over a twelve-bar chord progression
fact: The minor pentatonic scale has five notes; in A, they are A, C, D, E and G, and many blues solos are built from it.
story:
John's grandfather kept an old guitar behind the kitchen door, and every summer visit John had looked at it without daring to touch it. This year was different, because Mr. Yilmaz from next door had shown him three chords, and for two weeks John had played them until his fingertips stung. Now he wanted the other thing, the thing he heard on his grandfather's scratchy records: the singing lines that curled over the chords like smoke.

"You're not going to learn that from staring," said Margo, who had ridden her bike over because she was bored and curious in equal parts. She sat on the porch rail, recording him on her phone. "I'll narrate the video, like a nature documentary. Here we see the rare teenage guitarist, afraid to leave his habitat of three chords."

"Quiet," John said, but he was smiling. He played the twelve bars, A to D to A to E and around again, and then tried to make up a melody on top. It came out tangled, wrong notes crowding in like the invasive ivy that was swallowing his grandfather's fence, creeping over everything whether he wanted it or not. Margo winced, loudly, and he stopped.

Then he went inside and found his grandfather by the record player, turning a sleeve over in his hands. On the back, someone had written a list in faded pencil: A, C, D, E, G. "What's this?" John asked. His grandfather squinted at it. "Five notes," he said. "The minor pentatonic scale, they called it at the store. Fella said you build most blues solos out of those. In A, that's the set." He tapped the list with one crooked finger. "Any of those five will fit, he told me. Any one of them. That's the whole trick, and it's still a trick to me."

John carried the paper back to the porch, heart drumming. He played the progression again, and this time, when the moment came, he picked just one of the five notes and let it hang there. It fit. He picked another, slid it up a little, and it fit too, ragged but right, like the propeller on his grandfather's old model plane catching at last and pulling the whole thing into the air. Margo stopped narrating. For a whole chorus, John wandered through A, C, D, E and G, sometimes clumsy, sometimes sweet, never lost.

"That last part," Margo said quietly, still holding the phone up. "Do that again."

activity: to read a Shakespeare scene and paraphrase the speeches into modern English
knowledge_domain: to read a Shakespeare scene and paraphrase the speeches into modern English
fact: In Shakespeare's time, thou was used for close friends, family or people of lower rank, and sometimes as an insult, while you was the polite form for superiors and strangers.
story:
Jack sat at his grandfather's kitchen table with the Romeo and Juliet scene spread out in front of him, three days before he had to interpret it for Ms. Castillo's class. The assignment sounded simple. Read the speech, then say it again in normal words. The problem was that Tybalt's lines refused to become normal words.

"You can use my phone if you want to look things up," his grandfather said from the stove, "but the Wi-Fi is vain and proud and only works near the toaster."

"Wi-Fi can't be vain, Grandpa."

"Neither can a rooster, but look at ours."

Jack pulled his phone out anyway. His signal died two bars from the table, which felt personal. He texted Sulaiman, who had Ms. Castillo last period, and got back only a shrug emoji. Lyam sent him a picture of a dog in a raincoat. Helpful. Jack was on his own.

He copied Tybalt's lines onto a napkin and read them out loud, trying each one as modern speech. Then he noticed something odd, like a knot in wood you only see once you're sanding it. At the start of the argument, Tybalt says you to Mercutio. Polite. Frosty, even. Then, halfway down the page, after the insults start flying, every you turns into thou. Jack counted. Four switches, all in one direction. He flipped back to the balcony scene, where Romeo talks to Juliet, and there it was again, thou, thou, thou, the whole way through.

"Sulaiman, come on, I know you're reading these," Jack muttered. He tried an experiment. If thou showed up for people you were close to, like Romeo and Juliet, then Tybalt switching to thou mid-fight would be like calling Mercutio "buddy" with your fists already up. A drop in rank. In Shakespeare's time, you was the polite form for superiors and strangers, and thou was for close friends, family, people beneath you, or an insult when you hurled it. So Tybalt wasn't getting coarser by accident. He was demoting Mercutio on purpose, right in front of everyone. No wonder the fight started. The word itself was the slap.

Jack wrote his paraphrase fast, then read it to his grandfather, who leaned against the counter with a wooden spoon like a microphone. When Jack delivered Tybalt's line as, "You're nothing to me, so don't talk to me like we're friends," his grandfather winced theatrically.

"I've had arguments like that with the rooster," he said. "He starts out respectful, then it's thou, thou, thou all morning."

"Did you feel resentment toward the rooster, Grandpa?"

"I felt the rooster had resentment toward me."

There was a knock at the screen door. Sulaiman stood on the porch holding his laptop, out of breath, having run the four blocks from his house. "Okay, so I asked Ms. Castillo what happens if you get the paraphrase wrong, and she said, and I quote, 'nothing terrible, I just want you to think.' But then she smiled, and Jack, it was a scary smile."

Jack held up the napkin with the arrows and the counts. "Look. Watch what happens at line ninety."

Sulaiman read it, and his eyebrows went up exactly the way Jack's had. "He drops the you. Oh, that's so rude."

"That's the whole fight," Jack said, and slid the napkin across the table toward him.

activity: going to a first school dance
knowledge_domain: going to a first school dance
fact: A glow stick shines brighter but runs out faster when it is warm, and glows dimmer but lasts longer when it is cold.
story:
Dominic stood in the aisle of Hollister's, a clothing store, holding two shirts and deciding which one would make Malcom stop laughing at him. The dance was Friday, his first one, and the invitation had said something about a glow theme. His mother had said a collared shirt was mandatory, which ruled out the black T-shirt with the dragon on it, so the choice was between a blue button-down and a green one.

"Blue," said Theresa, appearing beside him with a basket. "Green makes you look like a lime." She pulled a package of glow sticks off a rack near the register and dropped it in. "Fifty for four dollars. We're splitting them for the dance."

Dominic paid for the blue shirt and his share of the glow sticks. On the way out, he noticed the cashier had set the basket of glow sticks near the door, where the afternoon sun came through the glass and warmed them. He almost said something, then didn't, because he wasn't sure yet what he wanted to say.

At the dance on Friday, the gym was hot. Dominic cracked his glow stick, and it blazed so bright it lit up his whole hand, brighter than Theresa's or Malcom's. "Look at that," Malcom said. But by the time the slow songs started, Dominic's stick had faded to a dull smudge, while Theresa's, cracked later and kept in her jacket pocket near the cold door, still burned a steady orange. Dominic turned his dark stick over and thought about the sunny basket by the store door. He had cracked his first, in the warmest corner of the gym, and it had spent everything at once.

He tested the idea at intermission. He put two fresh sticks from his pocket in the drinks cooler where the ice chests sat, waited ten minutes, cracked one, and compared it to the room-temperature one Malcom held. The cold one glowed dimmer, a soft green instead of a shout, but Malcom's warm one was already weakening after twenty minutes while the cold one stayed steady through the last hour of the dance.

Theresa wrote him a note on the bus home and passed it over the seat. "My stick from the freezer test," it said, meaning the one she had stuck in a cup of ice. "Still glowing dim. Yours dead. Coincidence? Bring your stick Monday, we'll try the freezer at my house, see if it's still going in the morning."

On Saturday morning Dominic found the glow stick Theresa had left in his mailbox with a rubber band around it, because his instinct had been to say no, that the whole thing was silly, but her note had a point. He took it inside, held it up to the kitchen window, and saw the faint green still alive inside the plastic.

"It made it," he told his mother. "It's dimmer than anything at the dance, but it's the only one still going."

His mother looked over his shoulder. "So the freezer really does keep them alive longer?"

"That's the plan," Dominic said. "Theresa wants to time the next one. Monday, six a.m., my kitchen."

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: Deleting a post removes it from your page, but anyone who already took a screenshot or saved a copy still has it.
story:
The photo went up at 9:14 on a Tuesday night: Victor doing a failed backflip off the gym bleachers, legs bent, face frozen in pure panic. He had meant to send it to Zackary only, but his thumb slipped, and there it was on his story for everyone. He deleted it after ten minutes and lay back on his bed, telling himself it was gone.

It was not gone. The next morning the eighth-grade group chat, forty-three people deep, lit up with the same photo, reposted by someone Victor didn't even know. Naila had screenshotted it before it vanished. "It disappeared from your page so fast," she typed, with a crying-laughing emoji. "Good thing deleting a post doesn't do anything about everyone who already saved a copy."

Victor stared at that sentence. He thought of last summer, when his older cousin had told him about a pool-party video that got someone uninvited from a whole birthday trip, weeks after it was taken down. Victor hadn't believed it mattered back then. He believed it now. He scrolled the chat and counted: the photo had already been reposted three separate times, by three people, none of whom had been his friends a year ago.

At lunch he found Zackary at the corner table and slid his phone across the tray. "Test something with me," Victor said. "I'll post a dumb picture of my shoe, delete it after ten minutes, and we watch what happens." Zackary, who was usually the first to laugh at Victor's disasters, agreed. They posted a photo of Victor's gray sneaker with the caption "the legend." Victor deleted it on schedule. Then he waited, and by sixth period the shoe had appeared in the same group chat, forwarded twice, captioned "whose funeral is this."

It should have made him feel better, proving the rule, but it made him feel worse, because the rule had no exceptions. He tried to think of a fix. He could ask Naila to take her copy down, but he couldn't ask the strangers. He could stay out of that chat, but the chat wasn't really a place, it was a copy machine. "So nothing ever really deletes," Zackary said, chewing the last of his fries. Victor turned his phone face down on the table, then flipped it over again, because he couldn't stop checking.

In English, Mr. Hughes was talking about how news stories can carry bias, how a single angle on a person can harden into a reputation. Victor raised his hand. "Could a photo do that? Even if the person took it down?" Mr. Hughes paused, one chalk-dusted finger in the air. "Now that," he said, "is an agile question." Victor wrote nothing down. Outside the window, someone on the track team cleared a hurdle, and Victor thought, that's the trick, maybe: not to stop falling, just to get better at landing. His phone buzzed once in his pocket. He left it there.
