fact: Specific details, like 'Grandma's red bicycle' instead of 'a bike', give an improv partner more to build on.
story:
Jonathan got the slip of paper on Monday: his drama class would perform short improvised scenes at Friday's assembly, and his partner was Jan. In class, Ms. Clarke wrote two words on the board, "yes, and," and said that whatever your partner offered, you agreed to it and added something of your own. Then she gave them ten minutes to practice in the hallway.

Jan started a scene. "I'm cleaning out the garage," she said, lifting an invisible box.

"Yes, and, there's some stuff in it," Jonathan said.

"Yes, and, there's other stuff too," Jan said. They dragged invisible boxes around for two more turns and then Jan stopped. "This is going nowhere. We have nothing to work with." They tried again and got the same flat result, and the bell rang before they could fix it.

At lunch Jonathan sat with Lyndon and thought about what had gone wrong. The pattern couldn't be in the boxes, since the boxes weren't real. It had to be in the words. When Jan said "the garage," he could see a garage, but "some stuff" was just fog. He thought of his grandmother's red bicycle, which sat in her hallway because she wouldn't ride it after her knee surgery. He hadn't seen it in months, but the moment he pictured it, he knew exactly how to describe it. He decided to test the idea at practice after school: instead of saying "a bike," he would name a specific one.

They met in the music room. "I'm cleaning out the garage," Jan said again.

"Yes, and, I found Grandma's red bicycle," Jonathan said, gripping imaginary handlebars.

Jan's face changed. "Yes, and, she said she'd never give it away, so we have to hide it before the yard sale," she said, wheeling it behind an invisible shelf. "Yes, and, the buyer is coming in five minutes, so we have to postpone the sale with a vigorous speech about how the garage is haunted." She stood on a chair and delivered the speech, waving both arms, and Jonathan laughed so hard he forgot his next line, which somehow fit the scene anyway.

They ran it twice more, and each time a named object, a photo album from 1974, a jar of marbles labelled "TEETH," pulled the scene forward. On Friday they stood behind the curtain, the assembly noise humming through the gym like a network of static, all those separate conversations joined into one sound. The curtain opened. Jan lifted the invisible box. "I'm cleaning out the garage."

"Yes, and," Jonathan said, "I found Grandma's red bicycle."

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
knowledge_domain: recovering from a cold or flu at home
fact: According to the U.S. CDC, people with the flu are most contagious during the first three days of their illness.
story:
Lincoln sat at the kitchen table with a mug of tea going cold beside him and his phone propped against the sugar bowl. It was day two of the flu, and he already felt almost human again. His fever was gone, his voice had come back, and best of all, Josiah's birthday party was tomorrow night. He dragged the spoon through his untouched soup and decided he was going.

A text from Josiah came through while he was mentally picking out which shirt to wear. "Party's still on for Saturday. Nick's bringing his speakers. You in?" Lincoln typed "definitely" and then stopped, thumb hovering. His mom had said something that morning about him still being able to get other people sick, and she hadn't explained it, just left a printed page from the health department on the counter next to his soup. He picked it up, expecting a lecture about hand washing.

The page was from the U.S. CDC, and one line stopped him cold: people with the flu are most contagious during the first three days of their illness. He read it twice. Day one had been Wednesday, a miserable blur of fever and blankets. Thursday was day two. That made tomorrow day three. The last day of being the most contagious. He could feel fine, he realized, and still be handing the flu to every kid crowded around Nick's speakers. He imagined the virus starting to circulate through Josiah's whole basement, kid by kid, while he stood there feeling proud of his recovery.

He looked across the kitchen at his mom, who was washing the soup pot even though he hadn't eaten any of it. She didn't say "I told you so." She just said, "There's more soup if you want it later," and set a box of crackers quietly at his elbow.

Lincoln typed a new message. "Can't come Saturday. Flu. I'm on the last of my most contagious days, day three, so it's not worth gambling on. Next weekend though, I'll take you and Nick out for burgers, my treat." He hesitated, then added, "Don't share drinks at the party. You're welcome."

Josiah replied with a single thumbs-up, and then Nick sent a row of crying-laughing faces and the words "commerce at last, Lincoln paying." Lincoln grinned. He carried his mug to the microwave and reheated the tea, and when it beeped, he noticed his mom had already refilled the cracker box and left it back at his spot, next to the CDC page turned face down.

He sat, dipped a cracker into the soup he'd suddenly decided was worth eating, and texted Josiah one more thing: "Save me a corner of the cake. I'll collect it Monday, and I'll be so far past day three you won't even know I was sick."

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
knowledge_domain: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
fact: Parallel lines like railway tracks or the two edges of a road look as if they meet in the distance, even though they never actually meet.
story:
Emile sat in Mr. Warsame's art room, glaring at his drawing of Main Street, which looked like a street designed by a committee that hated each other. The buildings leaned. The road lay flat as a pancake. Mr. Warsame leaned over his shoulder and said only, "Pick one dot, Emile. Make every line obey it." Then he moved on, which was not helpful, because Emile did not know what the dot was for.

At lunch, Charleigh studied the drawing with narrowed eyes, assessing it like a detective at a crime scene. "It looks like the buildings are falling on each other," she said. Mahi squinted too. "Maybe the road needs to shrink? Roads get skinnier far away. Like train tracks." Emile was skeptical. "Tracks don't shrink. They're stuck to the ground. You'd have trains wobbling all over the place." Mahi grinned. "Come on. There's a footbridge over the tracks. We'll look."

The three of them stood on the quiet footbridge after school, a whole parliament of pigeons muttering below on the gravel. The tracks ran straight out beneath them toward the horizon. "See?" Mahi said, pointing. "They touch." Emile stared hard. The two rails did seem to lean toward each other, narrowing and narrowing until they met at a single trembling point far away, like a zipper closing. "They can't touch," Emile said. "They're parallel. Parallel lines never actually meet. They just look like they do." But his eyes kept insisting otherwise, and that was the strange part: his eyes and his brain were having an argument, and his eyes were winning.

He crouched and looked down the tracks again. Then he held up his pencil at arm's length, like a tiny ruler, and measured the rails near the bridge. Two fingers apart. He measured where they "met." His fingers pinched to nothing. It was like a magic trick where the magician shows you both ends and you still can't find the seam. "Wait," he said slowly. "The rails don't get closer. But if I draw them going to one point anyway..." He trailed off, already running scenes in his head: the dot on his paper, every edge of the street and every window marching toward it, like the whole city was being poured through a funnel.

Back in the art room the next day, Emile drew his dot in the middle of the page and named it out loud, half to the paper and half to the ceiling: "You're the vanishing point." Then he ruled lines to it from every corner. The road dropped into it. The buildings grew out of it. Even the pigeons, which had somehow followed him and were now holding a full parliament debate on the windowsill, would have approved.

Mr. Warsame stopped behind him. "There's one problem," he said. Emile froze. "You've drawn a pigeon standing on your vanishing point." Emile leaned closer. Sure enough, a smudge sat exactly on the dot, with two little legs and a beak. "That," Emile said, "is the mayor of my street." He drew a tiny crown on it.

activity: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
knowledge_domain: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
fact: In improv, 'yes, and' means accepting what your partner has established (yes) and then adding something new to it (and).
story:
Jacob sat on the living room rug with his laptop open, watching the drama camp video for the third time. On Monday he'd have to improvise a scene with a partner, and the thought made his stomach fluctuate between excited and terrified like a fish flopping on a dock. He'd never done improv before. What if he froze?

Dania lived next door, so he texted her, and ten minutes later she was sitting on his couch with a bag of popcorn, willing to practice. "Just start something," she said, "and I'll jump in."

"Okay. You're a customer at my lemonade stand."

"You're an alien selling lemonade," she countered.

They did the scene. Every time she added something, he just nodded. "Yeah." "Sure." "Okay." After a minute they both stood there, staring at each other, the scene as dead as the popcorn crumbs at the bottom of the bag.

Jacob rewound the video. That was when he noticed the pattern: in every good scene, nobody just agreed. "See how he says 'yes, and'?" he asked, pointing at the screen. The actor said yes to whatever his partner had established, then added something new. In their failed scene, Jacob had done only the yes. Every yes with nothing after it was a locked door, and the scene had ground to a halt. He'd been so worried about being polite that he'd forgotten to build anything.

"One more time," he said. "You're a customer."

"You're an alien," Dania said, grinning, "and you charge three moons per cup."

"Yes, and today we're out of moons, so you can pay in secrets."

Dania laughed so hard she knocked over the popcorn. "Yes, and my secret is that I know where your flying saucer is parked."

"Impossible. It's immune to detection. It looks like a very boring minivan." The scene snowballed, each line handing the other one something new, and Jacob felt like he'd found the secret engine under the floor of the whole thing.

On Monday, Harper ended up being his partner. When Harper announced they were both trapped in a haunted refrigerator, Jacob didn't just shiver and nod. "Yes, and the ghost only speaks in knock-knock jokes," he said, and watched Harper's whole face light up.

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Feeling anxious sometimes is normal, but when anxiety is intense, lasts a long time and gets in the way of daily life, a doctor may diagnose an anxiety disorder, which is treatable.
story:
Scarlett had invited Jolene over to make a poster for their science project, but the poster had not been touched for twenty minutes because Jolene kept checking her phone.

"Can you put that away?" Scarlett asked. "We need to illustrate the water cycle with actual drawings."

"In a second." Jolene's thumb hovered over the screen. She was waiting for her mother to text back about her audition results, and she had checked the phone eleven times since arriving, because Scarlett had counted.

"You checked it before you knocked on my door," Scarlett said. "And in the kitchen, and twice on the couch." She had a theory forming, the kind you could test. Maybe the checking was not the problem itself but a symptom of something underneath, like a runny nose was not the cold but proof of one. "What happens if you don't look at it?"

"Nothing, probably." Jolene set the phone face down on the table, and then picked it up again nine seconds later. "I don't know. My stomach hurts and my heart goes fast and I keep thinking if I don't see the message the second it comes, something terrible will happen. It's been like this since Tuesday. I couldn't even eat the nutritious dinner my dad made last night, and he made the good chicken."

Scarlett thought of her own worry spikes, like before the spelling bee, and how those had faded by the next day. Jolene's had lasted four days and was wrecking her sleep and her appetite. That seemed like a different category of thing, not just nerves.

"Ariyah had something like this," Scarlett said slowly. She pulled up a text conversation and handed the phone over. Last spring Ariyah had written a whole paragraph about it, and Scarlett had read it three times.

Jolene read it out loud. "Feeling anxious sometimes is normal, but when it's intense, lasts a long time and gets in the way of your life, a doctor can diagnose an anxiety disorder. Mine is treatable. I told my doctor everything and it got so much better."

"A disorder," Jolene repeated. "That sounds serious."

"It sounds fixable," Scarlett said. "That's the part I'd care about. Ariyah told a doctor, and a doctor is literally somebody whose income depends on knowing this stuff. That's their whole job."

Jolene laughed for the first time all afternoon. She put the phone down again, and this time it stayed down while she picked up a blue marker and drew a lopsided cloud. "My mom gets home at six. Maybe I'll tell her I want to make an appointment. A real one, not the dentist kind."

They drew clouds and arrows until the doorbell rang. Jolene's phone lit up on the table with her audition results, and Scarlett realized neither of them had looked at it in half an hour.

"Are you going to check that?" she asked.

Jolene glanced at the glowing screen and shrugged. "It'll still say the same thing at six o'clock." She reached over and turned it face down, then went back to her cloud, the marker squeaking against the poster board.

activity: to describe how natural selection changed the beak shapes of finches on different islands
knowledge_domain: to describe how natural selection changed the beak shapes of finches on different islands
fact: Natural selection acts on individuals, but it is populations that evolve; a single finch cannot grow a bigger beak because it needs one.
story:
Ryder had exactly one hour before Mr. Wiśniewski collected the science journals, and his page on the Galápagos finches said, in its entirety, "Beaks. Different islands. The end."

"Deep stuff," said Rae, leaning over from the next desk. "You should write greeting cards."

"You're the one who said finches grew bigger beaks because they wanted to survive," Ryder whispered back. "I heard you."

"That's basically what happened. Drought hits, birds need tougher seeds, so they grow bigger beaks. Like a muscle."

Ryder squinted at his page. Something about that itched. He pictured a single finch on a dry island, staring at a hard seed, willing its own beak longer. "A bird can't just grow a bigger beak because it needs one," he said slowly. "Can it?"

"Then how did the beaks change?" Rae said. "Magic?"

Guillaume spun around from the front row, which he was only allowed to do because Mr. Wiśniewski had stepped into the supply closet. "Try it," he said. "Mr. Wiśniewski left the seed-sorting kit. Tweezers, pliers, crack hammer. Different beak components, different seeds. We can dismantle the whole question."

They did. At the back table, they set out three bowls: tiny soft seeds, medium ones, and rock-hard nuts that Guillaume claimed could survive an apocalypse. Ryder took the tweezers, Rae took the pliers, Guillaume took the hammer, because of course he did.

Thirty seconds of frantic grabbing later, the tweezers had collected two soft seeds and zero hard nuts. The pliers had crushed the middle bowl and even cracked a few nuts.

"So the tweezer bird just decides to have pliers," Rae said.

"No." Ryder stared at the bowls, feeling the idea click into place like a component snapping onto a model. "Look. The tweezer bird tries, the tweezer bird fails, the tweezer bird maybe doesn't make it. But somewhere in that flock, some birds already had plier-ish beaks, because they just do, everyone's a little different. Those are the ones that get the nuts and the chicks. Over time the whole island is full of plier beaks."

Rae frowned. "So nothing grew anything?"

"The individual finch doesn't change," Ryder said. "The population does. That's the difference."

Guillaume raised his hammer solemnly. "The population evolves. The individual just picks seeds badly."

Ryder grabbed his journal. That night he wrote a note and left it in Rae's locker before first period: "Dear Bird-Who-Wanted-a-Bigger-Beak. I am sorry evolution does not take requests. You personally are stuck with your beak. Your great-great-grandkids, however, will be extremely plier-shaped. Congratulations to them. Sincerely, a different individual in a changing population."

At lunch, Rae slapped the note onto the table beside his tray.

"Zero out of ten," Rae said. "I showed my dad. He laughed so hard he asked if he could keep it."

"Ten out of ten," said Guillaume, reaching for Rae's fries with the tweezers from his pencil case.

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: In science, a theory is not a guess; it is an explanation that has been repeatedly tested and supported, while a hypothesis is an idea still being tested.
story:
Abigail counted the lemon bars twice, and both times she got five when there should have been nine. She had left them cooling on the windowsill in the kitchen, gone upstairs for forty minutes to finish her math homework, and come back to a plate that looked robbed. Somebody in this house was a thief, and she intended to find out who.

"Maybe you miscounted when you made them," her brother said from the couch, not looking up from his phone. "Things like that happen. It's just a guess either way."

"It's not a guess if I can test it," Abigail said. She had learned that word from a video the class watched after a trip to the science centre, and it had stuck with her: a hypothesis was an idea still being tested, while a theory was an explanation that had been tested over and over and supported every time. A guess was something you couldn't do anything with. A hypothesis you could test. Her first one was simple: her brother was sneaking lemon bars while she was upstairs, because he had done it before with her birthday cake in March.

She refused to let him elaborate on his objections. Instead she set a trap that any spy would consider versatile: a thin, even layer of flour on the counter below the windowsill, invisible from a distance, ready to record whatever touched it. Then she baked a fresh batch, positioned it exactly where the old one had been, and announced loudly that she was going to her room for an hour. She even shut her door and put on headphones so he would think she couldn't hear anything.

An hour later, the plate had lost four bars again, and there were prints in the flour. Abigail crouched down with her phone flashlight and felt her whole hypothesis collapse. The prints were small, round, and arranged in a pattern no human shoes could make. They were paw prints, and they led to the window, which she had left open a crack because of the heat. The neighbor's orange cat, Mr. Lindqvist's cat, sat on the outside sill at that very moment, washing its face with the calm of a creature that had never once been caught.

"So it wasn't you," Abigail said to her brother, showing him the photos. "I was wrong, and I'm glad, because now I actually know something. That's how it's supposed to work. You test an idea, and if the test knocks it down, you get a better idea."

Her brother put his phone down, which was rare. "That's like what we argued about last week," he said slowly. "I said evolution was just a theory, like it was just a guess. But that's not what a theory is, is it?"

"No. A theory is an explanation that's been tested over and over and supported," Abigail said. "A hypothesis is an idea still being tested. Like my cat idea, before the flour." She closed the window, moved the plate to the top of the pantry, and wrote "Round Two" on a fresh sheet of notebook paper.

"Round two of what?" her brother asked.

"Of finding out whether anything in this house can open a pantry," she said, and dusted the flour off her hands.

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: Psychologist John Suler described the 'online disinhibition effect' in 2004: people often say things online that they would hold back from saying face to face.
story:
Aiden sat at the kitchen computer with his backpack still on one shoulder, refreshing the class discussion board for the third time. His group project thread had grown overnight, and near the bottom sat a comment from Reed: "This timeline is a mess. Did anyone actually read the assignment?" Aiden stared at it. Reed had lent him a pencil just yesterday and had said "no problem" with a smile when Aiden returned it snapped in half.

He scrolled up and down, comparing. Macey's comments were full of exclamation marks and little jokes, and even her corrections sounded cheerful. His own messages looked stiff, he thought, like a kid wearing a tie. When the doorbell rang, the dog's bark emitted from the hall in two sharp bursts, and Macey appeared at the screen door holding her tablet.

"Did you see what Reed wrote?" she asked.

"It doesn't even sound like him," Aiden said. He pulled up his saved screenshot. "In class he's the one who says 'good idea' even when the idea is mine and it's bad."

Macey leaned over his shoulder. "My mom calls it being two different people. Online Reed and hallway Reed."

Aiden wasn't sure that was fair. He opened the thread in another tab and counted: Reed had made four comments that day, and every one of them was blunter than anything he'd ever said out loud in a group. Aiden himself had typed things he'd later deleted, sentences he would never speak to someone's face. He turned that over while the computer's fan hummed beside him like a small sensor detecting his hesitation.

He decided to test something. Instead of typing a reply, he closed the tab and rode his bike to Reed's house. Reed answered the door holding a granola bar, and his face did the polite thing it always did.

"Hey, is something wrong with the timeline?" Aiden asked.

Reed blinked. "Oh. No, it's fine. I was up late and grumpy and it was easier to just type it." He rubbed the back of his neck. "I'd never say that to you guys in class."

They walked back to Aiden's, and on the way Reed explained, between bites, that his cousin had shown him an article once, written by a psychologist named John Suler in 2004, about the "online disinhibition effect," how people often say things online that they would hold back from saying face to face. Aiden filed the phrase away, thinking of his own deleted drafts.

At the kitchen computer they rebuilt the timeline together, Reed narrating politely out loud while Aiden typed, and when they finished, Reed dictated a comment to post: "Timeline is way better now, sorry about earlier." Then he added a smiley face, which Aiden had never once seen him draw on paper.

"Post it," Reed said, pointing at the button.

activity: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
knowledge_domain: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
fact: A settler's diary shows one person's view; it rarely tells how the Native American nations whose lands the trails crossed saw the same events.
story:
The assignment was due Friday, and Isabelle still had nothing except a textbook paragraph that put her to sleep. Mr. Moose had written one comment in red pen across her rough draft: "Use a primary source. A settler's diary would be strong."

So on Tuesday after school she rode her bike to the public library, where the local history room smelled like dust and old glue. Lilia came with her because Lilia always came with her, and because the vending machine near the copying desk sold the good pretzels.

The diary was in a gray archival box, and Mr. Moose, who shelved books there on Tuesdays, set it on the foam cradle and turned the pages with clean cotton gloves he handed to both girls so they could take turns. The settler's name was Ezra Pruitt. He had crossed in 1852, and his handwriting slanted forward as if he were hurrying even while writing.

"Land of milk and honey out here," Isabelle read aloud. "Fields a man could plow forever. Rain comes gentle most days." She frowned. "Wait. My textbook said precipitation was low on the plains. Ten inches a year, something like that. He says rain comes gentle most days."

"Maybe it rained the year he went," Lilia said, but she looked doubtful, and she pulled the climate chapter from her bag to check.

Isabelle kept reading. Ezra wrote about grass to the horizon, about oxen and fever, about his family. Then she flipped to the end, then back through the middle, hunting for something that never appeared. "He crossed all that land," she said slowly. "But there's nothing about the people already living on it. Not the nations whose lands the trails crossed. Not one page."

Lilia leaned over the cradle. "So it's like the rain thing. One guy's view, and it might not even be the whole weather picture."

"It's one person's view," Isabelle said. "The diary can't tell us how the Native American nations saw the same events. It just can't. It's only him."

She tested the idea on the way to the copier, holding her notes. If she used Ezra to explain why people moved west, she would have to say what her evidence could and could not show. She wrote a line at the top of her outline: powerful but one-sided. Ezra was influential evidence for what one settler believed, yet his silence implied that whole other side existed, whether he wrote it down or not.

At the desk, Mr. Moose slid the pretzel money Lilia had dropped back across the counter, and pointed them toward a shelf of oral histories told by Native American elders. "Might pair well," he said quietly.

Isabelle carried the first tape to the listening station and pressed play.

activity: to explain how nicotine causes addiction in the brain's reward pathway
knowledge_domain: to explain how nicotine causes addiction in the brain's reward pathway
fact: Nicotine works by fitting into nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, proteins on brain cells that normally respond to the brain's own chemical messenger, acetylcholine.
story:
Joshua locked the bathroom door and set his polymer clay model of a brain cell on the edge of the sink, where the fluorescent light hit the little bumps he had shaped into the membrane. The model looked symmetrical from the front, which was wrong, he realized now, because real receptors were lopsided, but there was no time to fix it. Mahi was picking him up in twenty minutes, and their science fair presentation was first period tomorrow.

He faced the mirror and began. "Nicotine gets into your brain and, um, it does stuff to your reward pathway."

He stopped. That was exactly what Mr. Rahman had circled in red on his notecard yesterday: "Do stuff? Explain how." Joshua leaned on the counter and stared at the receptor he had molded, the one with a slot down its middle. He had spent an hour on that slot without really knowing why it mattered. Then he remembered what Mahi had said while they were painting the poster board.

"Nicotine is like a fake key," she had said, tapping the drawing of the receptor. "It fits the lock."

He turned the model in his hands. A lock had a key that belonged to it. If nicotine was a fake key, then the real key was something the brain already had. He dug the crumpled library printout out of his backpack and smoothed it on the counter beside the soap dispenser. There it was. Acetylcholine. The brain's own chemical messenger. And the lock itself was a protein on the brain cell, a nicotinic acetylcholine receptor. He read the line twice, mouthing it.

"So the receptor is called a nicotinic acetylcholine receptor," he said to the mirror, "because it's a protein on the brain cell that normally responds to acetylcholine. Nicotine fits it too, like a fake key, and that's how it starts messing with the reward pathway." He said it again, slower, watching his own face to see whether he looked like he understood. The second time through, he did.

Someone knocked. "Joshua, are you rehearsing in there again?" his mom called.

"Ten more minutes!"

He heard Mahi's voice in the hall behind her. "It's me! I brought the notecards!"

He let her in, and she perched on the edge of the tub while he ran the whole explanation standing at the sink, holding the polymer clay receptor up like a tiny puppet. When he finished, she confided, "I was nervous you'd freeze up there tomorrow, but that actually worked."

"Freestyle it once," Joshua said, and turned on the faucet so the running water would be his audience noise.

He took a breath. "Inside your brain there's a lock on every cell. The real key is called acetylcholine. Nicotine is the fake one." He snapped the model into place on the cell and turned off the tap.

activity: competing in a spelling bee
knowledge_domain: competing in a spelling bee
fact: Noah Webster's 1828 'American Dictionary of the English Language' promoted simpler spellings such as 'color' instead of 'colour', which became standard in the United States.
story:
Jake sat in the third row of the library's community room, his hands folded on his knees the way Mr. Cohen had told him, and watched the word list in the moderator's hand like it was a snake that might strike. Twenty-two spellers had started the morning. Six were left. His word was coming, and the thing he wanted most in the world right now was to spell it right.

"Jake, your word is 'color'," the moderator said.

Something tickled the back of his mind. Two rows over, a boy named Kolten had just muttered to his cousin on the phone during the break, "It's not wrong, it's how they spell it in Canada." Kolten's cousin lived in Ottawa, and they'd been arguing about "colour" versus "color" until the librarian made them take it outside. Jake wondered about that. If the Canadians wrote it one way and Americans another, how did anyone know which one the bee wanted? The moderator was reading from an American dictionary, so probably "color." But why were there two spellings at all? That was the question that kept pulling at him, like a loose thread.

He asked for the definition. "A quality of light seen by the eye." He asked for the language of origin. "Latin." He asked if he could have a moment, which was mandatory before answering, though nobody ever said why. Then he took a breath and spelled it, "c-o-l-o-r," and the bell of the moderator's nod told him he was right.

Between rounds, Jake found Diana by the biography shelves. "Did you hear Kolten arguing about 'colour'?" he asked her. "Is that actually a word, or is his cousin just wrong?" Diana, who spent more time in the library than anyone Jake knew, pulled him toward the reference section. "There's an old dictionary back here. Mr. Cohen showed my class last year."

The book was enormous, with a cracked leather cover. Jake turned the brittle pages carefully, thinking it was a little like plumbing for words, a whole hidden system of pipes deciding where each spelling would flow. At the top of a page he found the entry. It was Noah Webster's 1828 dictionary, the American Dictionary of the English Language, and there it was: color, printed plain as day, spelled the American way. Diana leaned in. "It promoted simpler spellings like that. 'Color' instead of 'colour.' That's how it got standard here." Jake stared at the page. So that was it. The spelling Kolten's cousin used wasn't wrong at all; it was just the older pipe, the one that never got rerouted. Webster had rerouted it, and the whole country had followed.

"Round five," the moderator called. "Spellers to your seats."

Jake hurried back. Kolten was already seated, chewing his thumbnail, and Jake slid into the chair beside him. "Your cousin wasn't wrong," he whispered. "Canada just never got Webster." Kolten stared at him, and Jake grinned and pointed at the reference desk.

"Your word," the moderator said, and Kolten stood up straight.

"Catastrophe," she said.

activity: to write a thesis statement and outline a three-point argument before drafting
knowledge_domain: to write a thesis statement and outline a three-point argument before drafting
fact: An outline lists the main points and their evidence before drafting, so a writer can spot a weak or missing point before spending time on full paragraphs.
story:
Victoria stared at the blank page in her notebook and wrote a single sentence: School should start later. It had taken her ten minutes, and now Ms. Banerjee wanted an outline before anyone drafted a single paragraph.

"It's called a three-point argument," Ace said, leaning over from the next desk. "Thesis, then three points, then evidence under each one."

"That's the part I don't have," Victoria said. "Evidence."

She tried anyway, scribbling her three points on a napkin from lunch. Point one: teenagers are tired in the morning. Point two: later starts improve grades. Point three: buses could be rearranged. Under the first two she listed studies Ms. Banerjee had handed out last week. Under the third she wrote nothing.

Ace read it upside down. "Your third point is empty."

"It's obvious," Victoria said. "They'd just move the routes."

"Can you prove it?"

Victoria didn't answer. She folded the napkin and shoved it in her pocket, but at lunch she found herself pulling it out again beside Zachery, who was eating an extravagant pile of cafeteria fries, as usual.

"Give me one," she said.

"Get your own."

"For my outline. Point three, buses. I need evidence."

Zachery pushed the tray toward her and squinted at the napkin. "My mom drives for the district. She says they argue about routes every spring because of the middle schools. If they changed our start time, the whole schedule would fight with theirs."

"That's one person," Victoria said, but she wrote it down anyway.

That afternoon she tested it. She drafted a full paragraph on point three, the way she wanted to, four sentences of confident claims about buses. Then she looked back at the napkin. Three of her four sentences had nothing behind them, and she had just spent ten minutes writing them. If she'd checked first, she would have known.

She crossed the paragraph out and rewrote her outline on fresh paper. Under point three she wrote only what she could support, and then she found Zachery in the hallway.

"Can I quote your mom? Anonymously?"

"Sure. Why?"

"Because if I can't back it up, I shouldn't argue it." She hesitated, then decided to confide the rest. "My first idea was to just write it fancy and hope nobody noticed."

Zachery laughed so hard a freshman turned to stare.

At home, Victoria taped the napkin above her desk and wrote a note to herself on the back of a permission slip: New rule. Outline first. Every point needs its evidence before I start the paragraphs. Weak points get cut or fixed while they're still small.

The next morning she showed Ms. Banerjee the revised outline, with three points and something real under each one.

"Point two is your strongest," Ms. Banerjee said, tapping the page. "Consider making it your first body paragraph."

"Can I add a fourth point?"

"Only if you bring evidence by Friday."

Victoria sat down, opened her notebook, and wrote at the top of a clean page: Point four.

activity: to compare a first-past-the-post election with proportional representation using a sample vote count
knowledge_domain: to compare a first-past-the-post election with proportional representation using a sample vote count
fact: New Zealand voted in a 1993 referendum to replace first-past-the-post with a proportional system called MMP, and first used it in the 1996 election.
story:
Elizabeth had promised Naomy she would speak at the town hall meeting, and now that she was standing in line behind three adults and a man holding a poster about drains, she was trying to think of a way out of it.

The meeting was about the school council election. Ms. Goh had set it up so the whole town could hear the students argue, which did not intimidate the mayor, apparently, but did intimidate Elizabeth, who was twelve. The issue was simple. Their school used first-past-the-post, and Dion's group wanted proportional representation instead. Elizabeth's job was to defend the old system using the sample vote count Ms. Goh had printed on the whiteboard: 140 votes for Group A, 100 for Group B, 60 for Group C. Under the current rules, Group A won all five council seats.

"Under our system," Dion said into the microphone, "sixty people voted for Group C and got nothing. That's sixty people who might as well have stayed home."

"That's democracy," Elizabeth said when her turn came. "One round, one winner. It's simple." She was pleased with that until a woman near the front stood up.

"Has anywhere actually switched?" the woman asked. "Not talked about it. Done it."

Nobody answered. The man with the drain poster looked at his shoes. Elizabeth sat down next to Naomy and pulled out the tablet from the debate box, because she wanted to know too, and because a question you can't answer tends to follow you around.

She typed slowly, aware that Ms. Goh was watching the screen over her shoulder. New Zealand, she found. It had voted in a 1993 referendum to replace first-past-the-post with a proportional system called MMP. First used it in the 1996 election. She read it twice, then stood up again.

"It's been done," she said. "New Zealand. They voted in a referendum in 1993 to replace first-past-the-post with a proportional system called MMP, and they first used it in the 1996 election."

"Fine," Dion said. "So it's not inevitable that we stay with what we've got."

"It's also not inevitable that we switch," Elizabeth said. "They took three years just to get from the vote to the first election. That's longer than I've been at this school."

Somebody laughed. Ms. Goh wrote "sample count, next meeting" on the whiteboard and underlined it twice.

"Both of you bring numbers," she said. "No microbes of an argument. Full-grown ones."

"What's a microbe of an argument?" Naomy whispered.

"Something too small to see without a microscope," Elizabeth whispered back. "Like Dion's chance of beating me."

Dion, who had heard, held up the microphone and grinned. "See you Thursday."

activity: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
knowledge_domain: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
fact: Historians check a diary against other sources, such as letters, newspapers and government records, to test whether its details are accurate.
story:
The essay was due at eight the next morning, and Maya had one hour before her mom made her go to bed. She sat at the kitchen table with a photocopy of a settler's diary from 1847, three pages of faded looping handwriting, and a stack of library books she had lugged home through the rain. Her fingers still smelled of wet cardboard.

"Find anything good?" Tianna asked from the counter, where she was supposed to be studying for a math quiz but was actually drawing a horse on her binder. Tianna wanted an A on the quiz, but mostly she wanted the drawing to be good enough to show the art teacher tomorrow.

Maya tapped the diary. "This guy wrote that his family crossed the river on April the ninth because the ice finally broke. That's a perfect detail. I can use it to explain why people moved west, all that waiting for spring thaw." She copied the date onto her notepad and underlined it twice.

Then she found the newspaper. It was a scan of a frontier paper from the same town, the same month, and it reported that the river ice broke on April the nineteenth, ten days later than the diary said. Maya read both again. The room seemed to shrink around the two dates. If she used the diary and it was wrong, Ms. Pérez would ask how she knew, and she would have nothing.

She grabbed her phone and called Arman. "You have the government records, right? The ones you checked out?" He did, the land claims filed by settlers that spring. He read aloud while Maya held her breath, and there it was: the settler's own family had filed their crossing claim on April the nineteenth. The newspaper and the record agreed with each other. The diary was the one with the mistake.

"Wait," Arman said. "So the diary is useless?"

"No," Maya said slowly, watching the words on the page seem to shift. "Historians check a diary against other sources, like letters, newspapers and government records, to test whether its details are accurate. That's the whole point. He probably wrote it up later and misremembered the date. But his reasons for moving are still real, the failed crops, the cheap land. Only the detail's wrong." She crossed out April ninth and wrote the nineteenth, then started her first paragraph. The fog in her head that had made the whole assignment feel opaque began to lift, and her confidence, which had been dropping all evening, stopped its slide and rose again. The percentage of the essay left to write, she figured, was about ninety, and it was already past her deadline's halfway mark.

Tianna leaned over, horse forgotten. "You're going to finish by eight?"

"I have to," Maya said, and pulled the laptop toward her, keys already clicking.

activity: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
knowledge_domain: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
fact: Every formula in Excel or Google Sheets begins with an equals sign; without it, the cell just shows what was typed as text.
story:
Zack had promised Ms. Lewandowski his spreadsheet by the end of study hall, and so far his screen held exactly one thing: the words "SUM(B2:B10)" sitting in a cell like a bad joke, refusing to be a number. He had typed the class fundraiser numbers, ten rows of candy bar sales, and he wanted a total and a bar chart so the principal could see that Zack's group had sold more than any other. Instead, the cell showed what he typed, letter by letter, plain as a grocery list.

"You look like your dog died," said Theresa, leaning over from the next computer. The lab smelled of dry-erase markers and old radiator dust, and someone's sneakers squeaked against the tile behind them.

"My formula is broken. It just sits there." Zack pointed at the cell. "SUM(B2:B10). That's what it shows."

Yahia rolled his chair over, chewing the end of a pen cap. "That's not a total, that's a sentence about a total."

Zack stared at it. He tried deleting the last parenthesis and retyping it. Nothing. He clicked into another cell and typed 5+5, and the cell said 5+5 instead of 10. Then he noticed the cell next to it, one Yahia had made earlier, where a total actually lived. Yahia's cell started with an equals sign. Zack's didn't.

He sat up. Maybe the program couldn't tell the difference between words and math unless something marked it. Every formula in Yahia's column began with that sign; every plain typed thing Zack had made did not. He tested it, because testing things beat guessing. In a fresh cell he typed =5+5. The cell showed 10.

"Oh," Zack said quietly, and fixed his total: =SUM(B2:B10). The number 247 appeared, and it was so satisfying he almost elaborated out loud about it, but Yahia cut him off with "Chart, dude, three minutes left."

Zack highlighted the names and numbers, clicked the chart button, and bars sprang up across the screen like a small tsunami of data, their column towering over the others. Somewhere behind them, someone declared paper sign-up sheets obsolete and slammed a laptop shut.

Ms. Lewandowski walked past and paused at Zack's screen. "Twenty-four seven?" she said, reading the total.

"Candy bars," Zack said. "Two hundred forty-seven candy bars."

activity: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
knowledge_domain: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
fact: North of the Arctic Circle, the Sun stays up for at least one full day around the June solstice, which is called the midnight sun.
story:
The museum's Earth Science Hall had a problem: the seasons demo was broken, and Alyssa was the junior volunteer who had to fill in for the two o'clock presentation. She stood at the table with a globe, a lamp, and a sign that read "Why Do We Have Seasons?" and she did not fully know the answer. Her friend Ashlynn had come along for the afternoon, mostly for the free planetarium pass, and was currently eating crackers on the stool beside the table.

"I'm going to say it's the tilt," Alyssa said. "The Earth's axis is tilted, so that has to matter. I just can't say how yet."

"You could tell them it's distance," Ashlynn offered. "Closer to the Sun means summer."

Alyssa shook her head. "Then the whole planet would have summer at the same time, and Australia has winter when we do. So it can't be distance. It's the tilt doing something." She needed proof she could show, not just claim, because the last time she'd guessed at an answer in class, Mr. Njoroge had made her look it up in front of everyone. She was not repeating that.

She switched on the lamp and held the globe so the North Pole tipped toward the light. The top of the globe lit up broadly; the bottom caught only a slanted, weaker glow. She tipped it the other way and the pattern flipped. Whatever governed summer and winter, she could see it changing with the tilt and not with anything else. She turned the globe in a slow circle, keeping the tilt pointed the same direction, and watched the north brighten and dim over the year.

Ashlynn pulled out her phone. "Wait, look at this. My cousin posted it from her trip. She says she took it at midnight."

The photo showed a landscape with the Sun sitting low near the horizon, well above it, with a clock in the corner reading 11:58 p.m. Alyssa stared at it. A Sun up at midnight. That meant the tilt had to be extreme in some places.

"Where was she?" Alyssa asked.

"North of the Arctic Circle," Ashlynn read from the caption. "She says the Sun stays up for at least one full day around the June solstice. It's called the midnight sun."

Alyssa set the globe down with the North Pole tipped hard toward the lamp. The pole itself was bathed in light, and as she spun the globe through a full day, the light never left the top. There it was. She grabbed the blank card for her presentation and wrote in marker: The tilt points one hemisphere at the Sun. That hemisphere gets more direct light, and longer days. Above the Arctic Circle in June, the Sun does not set at all.

At two o'clock, a cluster of visitors gathered, including a man with two kids who kept trying to spin the globe. Alyssa held up Ashlynn's phone with the midnight photo beside the lit globe.

"This was taken at midnight," she said, "north of the Arctic Circle, near the June solstice. Watch what happens when I spin the globe with the pole tipped toward the lamp."

The younger kid leaned in, eyes on the glowing pole. "It never goes dark up there," he said.

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: In experiments by psychologist Henri Tajfel, people favoured members of their own group even when the groups had been assigned completely at random.
story:
Nathaniel's thumb hovered over the group chat, which had gone from forty messages a day to a sparse three, all of them from Japji. The chat was called Team Redraw, and it had started the week of the science fair, when Mr. Esposito had pulled names from a bowl to split the class into project teams. Nathaniel, Japji, and Timothe had landed together, and for two glorious days they had called themselves the luckiest group in the room. Then the teams had started acting like the teams mattered more than they did. Team Zenith had made matching profile pictures. Team Redraw's own chat was full of jokes about how Zenith's project was going to flop.

The problem Nathaniel wanted to solve was simpler than the project itself: everyone in the class had started saying "we" and "they" as if the bowl of names had sorted them into something real. He wanted his friends back, the ones who ate lunch with whoever was closest instead of whoever shared a team colour.

In the chat, Japji posted a link. "Look at this. A psychologist named Henri Tajfel did experiments where he put people into groups completely at random, and they still favoured their own group."

"Random how?" Timothe typed back.

"Like coin flips," Japji wrote. "No reason at all. And people still gave more to their own group."

Nathaniel read it twice. That was the hidden rule he had been half sensing all week, and now he had a name for the shape of it. If even random groups did this, then the bowl of names hadn't created a real division. It had just created a line, and everyone had agreed to see the line. He decided to test it.

He monitored the chat for a day, counting the "we versus them" messages: eleven. Then he posted a plan. "Science fair is in two days. What if our project is this? We split the class again, by drawing names from a hat, and see what happens."

Mr. Esposito agreed, probably because it was the first time anyone had proposed an actual experiment instead of a volcano. On Thursday, the class drew new names. Timothe landed on Zenith. A girl from Zenith joined Team Redraw. By lunch, Timothe was defending Zenith's tri-fold poster, and the girl was telling Nathaniel that Redraw's volcano genre of project was overdone, which it was.

"So the groups aren't real," Japji said, walking out with him. "They're just whoever the hat said."

"Right," Nathaniel said. "And the hat says something different every time."

Japji grinned and pulled out his phone. In the chat, he changed the group name to Everyone, and typed one line: "New rule. Whoever's closest at lunch, that's the team."
